We can use reported speech to inform what someone else says or said.
He told us that thanks to the change of focus on the defect tracking process.
The flow diagram reported that the development team had to enter and keep track of unnecessary information about the defects.
The team in charge of analyzing the flow diagram stated that our main flaws emerged from the design process since it is during this stage that the majority of the defects are injected.

We need to take into account two things when using reported speech. First, in the reported speech, the verb tenses change depending on the verb that introduces the reported statement; and second, we are going to use ‘that’ to introduce the reported sentence.

Example:

The experts say that organizations should track the most valuable data.   

For the reported speech, the most common verbs we are going to use are ‘say’ and ‘tell’. We use ‘say’ when we do not mention the person who the speaker is talking to like in the previous example. If we use the verb ‘tell’, we are going to clarify who the speaker is talking to. 

Example:

The experts told the software development team that organizations should track the most valuable data.

Nevertheless, we can have other verbs in the reported speech such as state, mention, advice, recommend, promise, and other verbs that can introduce what another person says.

Moreover, we have to take into account that the verb tenses will depend on the tense of the verb we use to introduce the reported speech. 

Examples:

The project manager says that it is necessary to track defects properly. 

The project manager said that it was necessary to track defects properly.  

Notice that sometimes you can use the same tense in reported speech, but most of the times the tense changes. Take a look at the following table to see how the tenses change.

Writing an Outline for a Text
An outline is a structure that summarizes the main ideas and arguments that are going to be part of a larger text.

Here are some steps you can follow for writing an outline:

  1. Choose a topic and purpose of your text: Knowing exactly what the text is being written for will help you to keep your aim in mind and avoid entering unrelated subjects or breaking the line of reasoning. If the topic and the purpose are clear, you can easily write an organized text.
  2. Develop a list of points to talk about: For this step, you need to be creative and start thinking about the ideas you are going to be developing in the text. Make sure you explore as many options and arguments as possible and give priority to those you think are most important and are able to back up the purpose of your text.
  3. Organize your main points: Once you have decided what arguments are going to guide your text, you need to make sure that the order in which you present them is comprehensible, easy to follow and set in such a way that one argument can be logically followed by the next one.
  4. Elaborate your main points: Now that you have decided the order of your main points or arguments, think about how to develop them and make them convincing. You can think about examples, theories, facts, quotes, or anecdotes. Be creative with the resources you use, but keep in mind that they should be relevant and support your argument and purpose of the text.
  5. Review and adjust: It is always important to go back and review the text. This is going to help you correct many mistakes and reconsider some aspects of the text.

images.text: I'm glad we reduced the amount of defects that were being tracked. The manager is very pleased with the new results we're getting. He told us that thanks to the change of focus on the defect tracking process, we're now being able not only to reduce the amount of time this process takes but also improve its effectiveness and productivity.

Last period, we assessed the performance of certain processes that the organization was undertaking. For instance, the flow diagram reported that the development team had to enter and keep track of unnecessary information about the defects, and this tedious process was delaying and affecting the overall performance of the project. For this reason, we agreed to take action and differentiate between the valuable data and the non-valuable data. As the team now focuses on the information that is truly useful, it is encouraged to track defects more consistently and therefore, improve the agility of the development and the quality of the product since more defects are being tracked and fixed.

The team in charge of analyzing the flow diagram stated that our main flaws emerged from the design process since it is during this stage that the majority of the defects are injected. Therefore, we're making sure this process is being assessed more often, and the Design Department informed that they were going to plan a reorganization of their activities. Some experts say that it is more profitable to focus on the sources of the potentially more costly defects and make sure to fix them in the early stages than to attempt to track every single defect along the life cycle of the product. This can be time-consuming and wind up being less productive at the end.
